raw_case_text:
A 14-year-old Sri Lankan male was admitted with five days of high-grade fever, myalgia and reduced urine output for two days. His past medical and family history was unremarkable. He reported exposure to stagnant water in a paddy field approximately two weeks before presentation.
On examination, his temperature was 38.1  C. The blood pressure was 90/50 mmHg, and the pulse rate was 112 beats per minute. This blood pressure was low for his age and sex, with the systolic and diastolic pressures corresponding to the 1st and 11th percentiles, respectively. His height was 177 cm, corresponding to the 87.5th percentile. The respiratory and neurological examination was unremarkable. There was no icterus, mucosal or conjunctival haemorrhages.
The initial investigations revealed a total leucocyte count of 18 x 103/mul (reference: -4,11), a platelet count of 54 x 103/mul (150 - 450), and a normal haemoglobin. His C reactive protein (CRP) was 232 mg/dl (<6), and the serum creatinine was 2.46 mg/dl (0.4 - 1.1). There was no evidence of liver injury or coagulopathy. Leptospirosis was confirmed with a microscopic agglutination test (MAT) titre of 1:160. Blood cultures and microbiological evaluation for Mycoplasma, COVID-19 and influenza were negative.
He was treated with intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone 1 g 12 hourly. We managed the acute kidney injury conservatively by maintaining the potassium, fluid and acid-base balance. The maximum serum creatinine (4.8 mg/dl) occurred on the eighth day of illness. The patient did not require renal replacement therapy.
On day six of illness, the patient developed acute pulmonary haemorrhage evidenced by declining oxygen saturation, bilateral fluffy shadows in the lung fields (see supplementary material 1 for high resolution computed tomography (HRCT) images) and a dropping haemoglobin level. We intubated and mechanically ventilated the patient for type 1 respiratory failure. We followed the standard protocol of five cycles of daily plasma exchanges (60 mL/kg, using fresh frozen plasma) and intra-nasal desmopressin (20 microg, six hourly) for leptospirosis pulmonary haemorrhage syndrome. We did not treat him with IV corticosteroids.
By the 12th day of illness, the patient was clinically improving with reducing ventilatory support requirement. The serum creatinine approached the baseline, and the urine output improved. We extubated him on the 13th day of illness.
On the 14th day of illness, the patient acutely became confused and agitated. A few hours later, he developed a generalised tonic-clonic convulsion lasting for 2 min, followed by post-ictal drowsiness. We reintubated him to maintain the airway.
His blood pressure was 140/90 mmHg, corresponding to the 98th and 99th percentiles for systolic and diastolic pressure, respectively. There was no neck stiffness or papilledema. His serum sodium was 138 mmol/L (135 - 145), and his blood glucose was 148 mg/dl (70 - 180). Calcium and magnesium levels were normal. There were bilateral occipital white matter hypodensities in the non-contrast CT scan of the brain. MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of the brain revealed bilateral symmetrical T2 signal hyperintensities in the occipito-parietal white matter compatible with PRES (Fig. 1). There were no features of vasculitis in the magnetic resonance angiogram (MRA) or evidence of cerebral venous thrombosis in the magnetic resonance venogram (MRV). Because we made a positive diagnosis of PRES, we did not perform a lumbar puncture.
We reduced the blood pressure to 110/80 mmHg and maintained that with IV labetalol. His consciousness improved over 24 h, after which we extubated him.
The patient did not develop any further seizures or neurological sequelae. Follow-up neuroimaging was normal at 3 months. The patient had an uneventful recovery. The timeline of events is given in Fig. 2.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 14-year-old male presenting with high-grade fever and myalgias for 5 days, and reduced urine output for 2 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began 5 days prior to admission with acute high-grade fever and generalized myalgias, followed 2 days prior to presentation by progressive oliguria. On day 6 of illness, he developed acute pulmonary hemorrhage manifested by dropping oxygen saturation, bilateral alveolar infiltrates, and falling hemoglobin, requiring mechanical ventilation for type 1 respiratory failure. Following extubation on illness day 13, he developed acute confusion, agitation, and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure on day 14.
subjective.past_medical_history: Past medical and family history was unremarkable. Epidemiological exposure: direct contact and exposure to stagnant water in a paddy field approximately 2 weeks prior to presentation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports high-grade fever, generalized myalgias, oliguria, confusion, and agitation. Home medications: none. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Upon admission: body temperature 38.1 °C, blood pressure 90/50 mmHg (1st percentile systolic, 11th percentile diastolic for age/sex), pulse rate 112 beats/min. Height 177 cm (87.5th percentile). Respiratory and neurological examinations initially unremarkable; no icterus, conjunctival suffusion, or mucosal hemorrhages. On day 14 (neurological event): blood pressure 140/90 mmHg (98th-99th percentile for age/sex), acute confusion, agitation, followed by a 2-minute generalized tonic-clonic convulsion and post-ictal drowsiness; no neck stiffness or papilledema.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: total leukocyte count 18 x 10^3/mcL (ref 4-11), platelet count 54 x 10^3/mcL (ref 150-450), normal initial hemoglobin (subsequently dropped during pulmonary hemorrhage). Inflammatory markers: C-reactive protein 232 mg/dL [or mg/L as written: '232 mg/dl (<6)']. Renal function & electrolytes: initial serum creatinine 2.46 mg/dL (ref 0.4-1.1), peaking at 4.8 mg/dL on illness day 8. Serum sodium 138 mmol/L (ref 135-145), blood glucose 148 mg/dL (ref 70-180), normal calcium and magnesium levels. Liver function and coagulation profile: normal. Microbiological workup: blood cultures negative; PCR/serology for Mycoplasma, COVID-19, and influenza negative.
objective.advanced_workup: High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of thorax: bilateral fluffy alveolar infiltrates indicative of acute pulmonary hemorrhage. Non-contrast brain CT: bilateral occipital white matter hypodensities. Brain MRI: bilateral symmetrical T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the occipitoparietal subcortical white matter, diagnostic of Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES). Magnetic resonance angiogram (MRA) and venogram (MRV): no evidence of cerebral vasculitis or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Lumbar puncture was omitted due to definitive imaging confirmation of PRES.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Leptospirosis confirmed by microscopic agglutination test (MAT) with a diagnostic titer of 1:160; complicated by severe leptospirosis pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome (type 1 respiratory failure), acute kidney injury (peak creatinine 4.8 mg/dL), severe thrombocytopenia, and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) manifested by acute hypertension and generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Negative evaluation for COVID-19, influenza, Mycoplasma, and bacterial pathogens ruled out alternate etiologies.
Plan & Treatment: Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g every 12 hours; conservative management of AKI with fluid and electrolyte titration (dialysis avoided); invasive mechanical ventilation for pulmonary hemorrhage managed with standard protocol of 5 daily cycles of therapeutic plasma exchange (60 mL/kg with fresh frozen plasma) and intranasal desmopressin (20 mcg q6h; corticosteroids withheld). For PRES: airway protection via re-intubation, IV labetalol infusion targeting blood pressure 110/80 mmHg.
Outcome: Rapid neurological recovery within 24 hours of blood pressure reduction; successful extubation; normalization of renal parameters; no recurrence of seizures; repeat neuroimaging at 3 months was completely normal with full recovery.
